records.text: Checklists Practical, repeatable checklists for using decision records — from deciding whether one is warranted, through writing, reviewing, and running the practice across an organization. Contents: Checklist: does this decision need a decision record? Checklist: before you start writing Checklist: while writing Checklist: before you publish for comment Checklist: review and approval Checklist: after the decision (rollout) Checklist: running decision records across an organization Checklist: quarterly or annual decision log audit Checklist: does this decision need a decision record? Write one if you answer yes to any of these: [ ] Would reversing this decision be costly, slow, or embarrassing? [ ] Does it affect people outside the room where it's being decided? [ ] Is it likely someone will ask "why did we do it this way?" a year from now? [ ] Are there genuinely contested options, with reasonable people on different sides? [ ] Does it set a precedent or policy other decisions will need to be consistent with? [ ] Would a new hire or a new leader in this role benefit from knowing the reasoning? Skip a decision record if all of these are true: [ ] It's cheap and fast to reverse. [ ] It affects only the decision-maker or a single self-contained team. [ ] It's already fully covered by existing policy, standard, or documentation. [ ] It's explicitly temporary — a workaround, pilot, or time-boxed experiment. Checklist: before you start writing [ ] Named decision-maker(s) identified — one person, or a specific committee/rule for how the group decides. [ ] Real stakeholders identified — who needs to weigh in before this is final? [ ] Deadline or urgency understood — does this have to be decided now, or can it wait for more information? [ ] Chose lightweight vs. comprehensive template based on stakes (see template/index.md). [ ] Know where the finished record will be stored, so it isn't lost in a chat thread or a single person's inbox. Checklist: while writing [ ] Title is short, present-tense, and active — states the decision, not the topic. [ ] Context explains the situation to a reader with zero meeting background. [ ] At least two genuinely viable options are listed, including "do nothing" if relevant. [ ] Each option's trade-offs are stated as facts, not as a strawman built to make the favored option win. [ ] Decision is written in plain active voice: "We will do X" — not a pros/cons summary standing in for a decision. [ ] Consequences describe what changes next, not a rehash of the options debate. [ ] Related decisions, requirements, or documents are linked, if any exist. [ ] The whole thing focuses on exactly one decision — split it if you find two. Checklist: before you publish for comment [ ] A stranger to the discussion could read it and understand both the decision and why. [ ] No unresolved "did you consider X?" gaps — if a likely question isn't answered, add it. [ ] Status is set correctly (usually request for comments or proposed at this stage). [ ] Comment deadline and process are stated explicitly (e.g., "comments by Friday, then default-accepted"). [ ] The record is one page or close to it — if it's sprawling, check whether it's actually more than one decision. Checklist: review and approval [ ] Every named stakeholder had a real chance to comment, not just a courtesy CC. [ ] Substantive comments are reflected in the record (as edits or as an added, dated note) — not just acknowledged and ignored. [ ] The named decision-maker explicitly accepted, rejected, or sent it back — silence is not acceptance. [ ] Status field is updated to match the outcome ( accepted , rejected , etc.) with a date. [ ] If rejected or deferred, the record still stays in the log rather than being deleted — it documents that the question was raised and why it didn't proceed. Checklist: after the decision (rollout) [ ] Decision is communicated to everyone it affects, not just those who were in the room. [ ] Follow-on requirements, budget, or training implications from the "Consequences" section are actually assigned to someone. [ ] The record is filed in the shared decision log, not left in a personal folder or a chat thread. [ ] An accountable owner is named for future review of this decision. [ ] If this decision supersedes a previous one, the old record's status is updated to superseded with a link forward. Checklist: running decision records across an organization [ ] Decided who can propose a decision record (commonly: anyone). [ ] Decided who can approve one, and whether that varies by decision type, dollar threshold, or risk level. [ ] Decided the escalation path when stakeholders disagree. [ ] Chosen a storage location every relevant team will actually use. [ ] Chosen a naming convention people can adopt without a program manager — "decisions" is often more approachable than "decision records." [ ] Identified a small number of early, high-visibility decisions to record first, to demonstrate value before mandating anything. [ ] Avoided turning this into forced paperwork — introduced it as something that makes a team's own life easier, not a top-down compliance requirement. Checklist: quarterly or annual decision log audit [ ] Skim for records stuck in request for comments or proposed with no resolution — close them out or explicitly archive them. [ ] Check that accepted decisions with a stated review cadence were actually reviewed. [ ] Check for decisions that were informally reversed in practice but never marked superseded in the log — update them. [ ] Spot-check a few older records: would a new hire today understand the context without asking someone? [ ] Confirm the log is still stored somewhere the current team actually uses — tooling and habits drift over a year.

records.title: Phase in the Agile Manifesto
records.text: Phase in the Agile Manifesto Status: accepted Date: 2026-02-16 Decision-maker(s): Chief Technology Officer Owner: Head of Delivery Context Our delivery teams work in long, planned projects with fixed scope and hand-offs between analysis, build, and test. Releases happen about twice a year, and customers often receive something that no longer matches what they need. Leaders want to adopt the values and principles of the Agile Manifesto: individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration, and responding to change. We have seen "agile transformations" fail when a ceremony is imposed without the underlying change, so we need a deliberate way to introduce it. Options considered Mandate a single agile method for all teams from next quarter. Quickest and most consistent, but it focuses on ceremonies, and teams that are not ready would perform them without changing how they work. Phase in by team, starting with volunteers. Start with two teams that want to try it, release in short cycles, and let them show the results; the manifesto's values are the guide and the specific practices are chosen by each team. Slower and uneven across the company, but it builds real examples and keeps the practices tied to the values. Hire an outside coaching firm to transform all teams. Brings experience and speed, but it is expensive and tends to leave when the engagement ends, with little capability inside the company. Decision We will phase in the Agile Manifesto by team: two volunteer teams in the first quarter, four more in the second, and the rest when the first six have run for two full quarters. Each team chooses its own practices, and we judge them against the manifesto's values and by delivery of working software to customers every two to four weeks. Consequences The Head of Delivery will support the volunteer teams, collect what they learn, and report to the CTO each quarter. Teams that have not yet moved will continue to work in the current way, so the organization will run two ways of working for about a year. Commitments to customers in fixed-scope contracts will not change automatically; we will handle each contract as it comes up for renewal. We will measure the time from an idea to working software in customers' hands, customer feedback, and team satisfaction, not the number of agile ceremonies. If the first teams do not show improvement after two quarters, we will stop and record what we learned before going further. Related See Phase in Extreme Programming for a decision on specific engineering practices that fit these values.

records.title: Phase in a business framework
records.text: Phase in a business framework Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-01 Decision-maker(s): CEO and executive team Owner: Chief of Staff Context Leadership wants to adopt Objectives and Key Results (OKRs) as our company-wide goal-setting framework, because teams currently set goals in different formats and cadences and leaders cannot see how team work connects to company priorities. Our last attempt to roll out a new planning process to all 240 employees at once stalled within two quarters: managers were not trained, the tooling was unsettled, and people treated it as extra reporting. We need to choose how to introduce the framework, not whether to. Options considered Big-bang rollout. Every team adopts OKRs at the start of the next quarter. Gets one shared language fastest and avoids running two systems side by side, but repeats the conditions that caused the last rollout to stall: no time to train managers, no proven examples, and no chance to fix the framework before everyone depends on it. Phased rollout over three quarters. Start with the executive team, add a small group of pilot departments, then extend company-wide. Costs about two additional quarters before every team is aligned, and for that time two goal-setting systems coexist, but each phase teaches us what to change before the next one. Adopt only at the executive level. Lowest effort and lowest risk, but it does not solve the visibility problem, since team goals would still be in different formats and cadences. Decision We will phase in OKRs over three quarters: the executive team in the first quarter, three pilot departments (Sales, Product, and Customer Support) in the second, and all remaining teams in the third. Each phase begins only when the exit criteria for the previous phase are met: leaders have been trained, goals have been scored at the end of a full cycle, and the pilot teams report that the process is worth the time it takes. Consequences The Chief of Staff will run the rollout, publish the exit criteria for each phase, and report progress to the executive team monthly. Until the third quarter, most teams keep their current goal-setting format, so company-wide visibility will be incomplete during the rollout. We accept this in exchange for fixing the framework before everyone depends on it. Pilot departments take on extra training and review time, which we will budget for explicitly rather than absorb silently. We will decide the tooling (a shared document or a dedicated product) at the end of the second quarter, using what the pilot teams actually needed, not before. If a phase's exit criteria are not met, we repeat that phase for another quarter instead of advancing; a follow-on decision will record any change to the plan. Related This decision does not change compensation or performance reviews; whether to link them to OKRs is a separate decision that we will not take until after the third phase.

records.title: Adopt contact relationship management
records.text: Adopt contact relationship management Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-12 Decision-maker(s): Chief Revenue Officer Owner: Head of Revenue Operations Context Our customer and partner contacts are held in individual inboxes, personal spreadsheets, and three different tools. When an account manager leaves, their relationships leave too, and we have twice contacted the same person on the same day from different teams. We also cannot show where in our organization a person's consent to be contacted is recorded. We need one shared way to manage contacts and our relationships with them, covering customers, partners, and suppliers, not only sales prospects. Options considered Keep the current mix of tools and spreadsheets. No cost or change effort, but the problems of lost relationships, duplicate contact, and unclear consent continue. Adopt one shared contact relationship management system for the whole company. One record per person and organization, a shared history of interactions, and recorded consent. Fixes the problems, but it needs data migration, rules for who may see what, and a change in habits from account managers. Add contact management to the existing sales CRM only. Quickest, and we know the tool, but it would leave partners and suppliers out and keep contacts held by non-sales teams separate. Decision We will adopt one shared contact relationship management system for the whole company, with one record per person and organization, a shared history of interactions, and the person's consent and contact preferences recorded on the record. We will migrate in stages, starting with the sales and customer support teams, and retire the other tools once their data has moved. Consequences The Head of Revenue Operations will lead the selection, the data migration, and the rules for who may see and change which records. Contact details and consent will be recorded in one place, and any request from a person to see, correct, or delete their data will be handled from that record. Account managers are expected to log their interactions in the system; we will check this in the first quarter and adjust the process, not just the reminders, if it is not happening. We will clean and merge duplicate contacts during migration, which will take staff time that we accept. We give up the freedom to use personal spreadsheets, in exchange for relationships that stay with the company and are easier to protect. Related See Select a CRM platform for the choice of a tool, which this decision builds on.

records.title: Phase in Extreme Programming
records.text: Phase in Extreme Programming Status: accepted Date: 2025-10-06 Decision-maker(s): Head of Engineering Owner: Engineering Manager Context Our product teams ship features in large batches, and defects found late are expensive: one in five releases needs a hotfix. We want to adopt practices from Extreme Programming (XP), such as test-driven development, pair programming, continuous integration, small releases, and collective code ownership. These practices support each other, but they also change how engineers work day to day, and adopting all of them at once is likely to meet resistance and to be done superficially. Options considered Adopt all of the practices at once in every team. The practices reinforce one another, but the change is large, and teams without the underlying skills would likely abandon them within weeks. Phase in the practices in a chosen order, team by team. Start with continuous integration and automated tests (the foundations), then small releases and pair programming, then test-driven development, with the teams adopting the practices at their own pace. Slower, but each practice has time to settle, and the early ones make the later ones possible. Adopt only the practices that are easy. Low effort, but it would skip the practices that give the largest benefit, such as automated testing, and the benefit would be small. Decision We will phase in XP practices in order: continuous integration and automated tests first, then small releases and pair programming, then test-driven development. One team begins in the first quarter, and each following team joins after the previous team has kept its release pipeline passing for a month. Consequences The Engineering Manager will coach the first team, publish what it learned, and track the share of releases that need a hotfix. Our target is to bring that share from one in five to below one in twenty within a year. Teams will have time for pairing and for writing tests built into their plans, and will not be expected to deliver the same number of features in the first quarter. Engineers keep a choice about how they pair and what tools they use; the practices set the outcome, not every detail of how it is reached. If a practice is not helping after two quarters, the team can propose to stop it, and we will record the reason. Related See Phase in the Agile Manifesto for the wider decision on values that these practices support.

records.title: Weigh health economics in a treatment funding decision
headings: Weigh health economics in a treatment funding decision
records.text: Weigh health economics in a treatment funding decision Status: accepted Date: 2026-05-12 Decision-maker(s): Regional commissioning board Owner: Director of Strategic Commissioning Context A new medicine for a chronic condition affecting about 6,000 people in our region has been proposed for funding. Trial evidence shows a modest improvement in quality of life and a reduction in hospital admissions, at a price of 9,500 per patient per year. Our budget is fixed, so funding it means funding something else less. A decision based only on the price or only on the clinical benefit would ignore that trade-off. We need to weigh the cost-effectiveness, the effect on the budget, and equity. Options considered Fund for all eligible patients. Gives every eligible patient access and is simple to run, but the budget impact (about 57 million a year at full uptake) would require cuts elsewhere, and the cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained is above our usual threshold. Do not fund. No budget impact and no displacement of other services, but patients lose a treatment with a demonstrated benefit and the decision may increase inequality for those without other options. Fund for a defined group with a managed-access agreement. Fund for the patients who benefit most (those with the highest admission rates), with the supplier lowering the price, collecting outcome data, and reviewing in three years. Brings the cost per QALY nearer to the threshold and limits the budget impact, but it excludes some patients and depends on the supplier agreeing and on data we can actually collect. Decision We will fund the medicine for the defined group under a managed-access agreement with a lower price, outcome data collection, and a review in three years. We make this decision on three considerations together: the incremental cost per QALY gained for the group, the budget impact over five years, and the effect on health inequalities. Consequences The Director of Strategic Commissioning will negotiate the agreement; if the supplier does not agree to the price and data terms, we will bring the decision back to the board. The budget impact is estimated at about 14 million a year at full uptake in the defined group; the board will name what is displaced, not leave it unstated. Patients outside the defined group will not be funded, and the eligibility criteria will be published with the reasons for them. We will measure admissions, quality of life, and uptake by deprivation group, and review the equity effect at the three-year review. We accept the risk that the group-level evidence is less certain than the overall trial evidence, and we will say so in the published rationale. Related See the Health Economics Guide for economic evaluation, budget impact, rationing, and equity.

records.title: Adopt a hybrid remote-work policy
records.text: Adopt a hybrid remote-work policy Status: accepted Date: 2026-01-08 Decision-maker(s): CEO and Head of People, with executive team input Owner: Head of People Summary: We will move from a fully-remote policy to a hybrid policy requiring two anchor days per week in-office for employees within commuting distance of a company office, effective next quarter. Issue Employee survey data over the last year shows a split: employees within commuting distance report reduced cross-team collaboration and slower onboarding for new hires, while fully-remote employees (outside commuting distance) report high satisfaction and cite remote flexibility as a top reason for joining. Leadership must decide whether to standardize a single policy or maintain a split arrangement, and if hybrid, how many anchor days to require. Assumptions In-office collaboration meaningfully improves onboarding speed and cross-team coordination for employees who can access an office, based on onboarding-time data comparing our two prior office cohorts. A policy requiring in-office days only for those within commuting distance is administrable without appearing arbitrary or unfair, if clearly documented. Real estate footprint is sufficient to support two-anchor-day attendance without added office investment. Constraints Cannot require relocation or in-office attendance for employees hired explicitly as fully-remote, per their offer terms. Any policy change must be communicated with at least one full quarter's notice. Legal has confirmed the policy must be applied consistently within each employee category to avoid discrimination exposure. Options considered Keep fully remote for everyone. Preserves current employee satisfaction scores and avoids a difficult policy change, but does not address the documented onboarding and collaboration gaps raised independently by three department heads. Require full-time in-office for all commuting-distance employees. Directly addresses collaboration and onboarding concerns, but survey data suggests this would trigger meaningful regretted attrition among employees who joined explicitly for remote flexibility. Hybrid: two anchor days per week for commuting-distance employees; fully remote unchanged for those outside commuting distance. Targets the specific population where the data shows a real gap, without changing terms for employees hired as fully remote. Argument The onboarding and collaboration data specifically implicates commuting-distance employees who are currently choosing not to come in, not remote employees generally. A blanket policy change would create attrition risk not supported by the data; a targeted hybrid policy addresses the actual gap while explicitly preserving the terms remote-hired employees joined under. Decision We will adopt a hybrid policy requiring two anchor days per week in-office for employees within commuting distance of a company office, effective next quarter. Employees hired explicitly as fully remote are unaffected. Implications Head of People will communicate the policy with a full quarter's notice, including which specific days are anchor days per office. Facilities will confirm office capacity supports two-day attendance without added real estate investment. Managers will need guidance on applying the policy consistently within their teams. People Operations will track onboarding-time and collaboration survey metrics for two quarters post-rollout to confirm the policy achieves its intended effect. This decision does not apply to future fully-remote offers unless a separate decision changes that hiring category going forward. Related decisions None superseded; this is the first formal remote-work policy decision recorded since the original all-remote transition three years ago (predates this decision log). Related notes Two department heads requested the policy include a stated review checkpoint rather than being open-ended; captured above as the two-quarter metric review.

records.title: Choose a hybrid working model
records.text: Choose a hybrid working model Status: accepted Date: 2026-08-20 Decision-maker(s): Executive team Owner: Chief People Officer Context Since 2021 our staff have worked mostly from home without a written policy, and different managers now expect different things. An engagement survey (response rate 81%) shows that 62% of staff want to work remotely at least three days a week, while several managers report that in-person days help onboarding and cross-team work. Our lease on the main office ends in 14 months and we have to decide how much space to keep. We need a hybrid working model that is clear, fair across roles, and affordable. Options considered Office-first. Everyone is in the office at least four days a week. Simple to explain and supports in-person learning, but it conflicts with what most staff say they want and narrows the talent we can hire from. Remote-first. No required office days, with a small space for meetings. Lowest property cost and the widest hiring pool, but it makes onboarding and cross-team work harder and leaves roles that cannot be done remotely in a separate category. Team-set anchor days. Each team chooses two or three shared in-person days a week that suit its work, inside company limits on minimum and maximum office time. Fits different kinds of work and keeps the benefits of being together, but it makes office capacity harder to plan and needs managers to apply the rules consistently. Decision We will adopt team-set anchor days: each team agrees in writing two to three shared in-person days a week, no team is required to be in the office more than three days, and the in-person days of each team are reviewed every six months. We will renew the lease for space that seats about 55% of staff on a typical day. Consequences The Chief People Officer publishes the policy, a template for a team's written agreement, and the rules on how to handle roles that cannot be done remotely. Managers are accountable for agreeing the anchor days with their teams and for applying the rules equally, and we will check this in the next engagement survey. Because only about 55% of staff are seated at a time, desks are booked rather than assigned; we accept that some staff will lose a fixed desk. Requests for different arrangements, for example because of a disability, follow Set a process for workplace reasonable adjustments rather than the team agreement. We give up the simplicity of one rule for everyone, in exchange for matching the arrangement to the work. Related This decision does not change pay or location-based allowances. Whether to link pay to work location is a separate decision.

records.title: Choose our information technology frameworks
records.text: Choose our information technology frameworks Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-14 Decision-maker(s): Chief Information Officer and Chief Technology Officer Owner: Head of Technology Operations Context Our technology group of 180 people has been asked by different leaders to adopt ITIL for service management, the Agile Manifesto for delivery, Extreme Programming for engineering, and Six Sigma for quality, sometimes in the same teams and in the same quarter. Each request is reasonable on its own, but together they overlap, use different vocabularies, and ask people to change how they work faster than they can absorb. We need to decide which frameworks we use, for which kinds of work, and in what order, so that teams get one coherent way of working and not four competing programs. Options considered Adopt every requested framework everywhere. Gives each sponsor what they asked for, but it overloads teams, produces conflicting guidance (for example, fixed change approvals versus continuous release), and makes it impossible to tell which change caused which result. Adopt one framework as the single standard. Simple to explain, but no single framework covers service operations, product delivery, engineering practice, and quality equally well, and the group would be forced to stretch one framework beyond what it was designed for. Assign each framework to the kind of work it fits, and phase them in one at a time. Use ITIL practices for running live services, the Agile Manifesto's values for how delivery teams plan and work, Extreme Programming practices for engineering teams that build software, and Six Sigma for processes where defects can be measured. Each framework is phased in separately with its own measures. Clearer for teams and easier to learn from, but it needs a written boundary between frameworks and takes about two years to complete. Decision We will assign each framework to the kind of work it fits and phase them in one at a time: first Agile Manifesto values for delivery teams, then ITIL practices for live services, then Extreme Programming practices for engineering teams, then Six Sigma for measurable processes. We will keep one short document that says which framework applies to which work and what takes precedence when guidance conflicts. Consequences The Head of Technology Operations will own the framework boundary document and settle conflicts between frameworks, with escalation to the CIO and CTO. We will start only one framework in a team at a time, and will not start the next until the previous one has met its own exit measures; the individual decisions follow the pattern in Phase in a business framework. Sponsors of the later frameworks will wait; we will tell them the order and the reason now, so that they can plan. Teams will use one shared vocabulary for the terms the frameworks share, such as incident, change, release, and defect, defined in the boundary document. We will review the whole approach after the first two frameworks, and revisit the order if the evidence shows a different one would have served us better. Related See Phase in the Agile Manifesto, Phase in ITIL 5, Phase in Extreme Programming, and Phase in Six Sigma for the decisions on each framework, and Phase in a business framework for the general pattern.

records.title: Phase in ITIL 5
records.text: Phase in ITIL 5 Status: accepted Date: 2026-09-30 Decision-maker(s): Chief Information Officer Owner: Head of IT Service Management Context Our IT service desk supports 3,200 staff and has grown without a common way of working: incidents, requests, and changes are handled in different ways by three teams, and recurring incidents are seldom analyzed. The CIO has chosen to base our IT service management on ITIL 5, the latest ITIL guidance, so that we share common practices and language with our suppliers and auditors. Adopting it at once across all teams would stop the service desk's own improvement work for months. We need to decide how to phase it in. This record describes our adoption plan and does not restate what ITIL 5 says. Options considered All at once. All teams adopt the chosen practices at the same time, so we have one way of working soonest, but the service desk has no capacity to retrain and to run the service in the same quarter, and we would be unable to adjust the practices to our context. Phase in by practice. Start with the practices that cause most pain and affect most users (incident and request handling), then change, then problem analysis and continual improvement, each in a separate phase with its own measures. Each phase lasts about a quarter and teaches us what to change next, but full adoption takes about a year and the old and new ways of working coexist for a time. Phase in by team. One team adopts all the practices first as a pilot, then the others follow. Gives a complete working example early, but it splits one service across two ways of working while the pilot runs, and that confuses users and suppliers. Decision We will phase in ITIL 5 by practice over four quarters: incident and request handling first, then change, then problem analysis, then continual improvement. A phase ends only when the previous phase's measures have been met for a full month: resolution time, first-time fix, and the share of changes that cause incidents. Consequences The Head of IT Service Management will lead the plan, publish the exit measures for each phase, and report to the CIO monthly. Staff will be trained in each practice just before its phase and not all at the start. For about a year, practices that have not yet been phased in will keep working in the current way, which we accept. Tooling changes are limited to what a phase requires; we will not buy a new service management platform until the end of the second phase and then decide with evidence. If a phase misses its measures, we repeat it for one more quarter and record the reason. Related See Phase in a business framework for the same approach applied to another framework.

records.title: Phase in lean manufacturing
records.text: Phase in lean manufacturing Status: accepted Date: 2025-11-24 Decision-maker(s): Plant Director Owner: Head of Operational Excellence Context Our plant makes custom industrial enclosures on four production lines. Lead times average 31 days against a customer expectation of 20, work-in-progress stock fills much of the floor, and surveys of operators suggest large amounts of waiting, rework, and movement of materials. Leaders want to adopt lean manufacturing, which focuses on removing waste and delivering what the customer values, but a plant-wide change at once would disrupt orders we must deliver this year. Options considered Change all four lines at once. The fastest route to a consistent plant, but it risks the delivery of current orders and gives the operators no time to learn and adjust. Phase in line by line, beginning with a pilot line. Start with one line, map its value stream, reduce waste, and use the results to choose practices for the rest. Disruption is contained and operators see real results before their own line changes, but full adoption takes about 18 months and the lines work in different ways for a time. Introduce lean tools plant-wide without redesigning the lines. For example, 5S (sort, set in order, shine, standardize, sustain) everywhere. Visible and cheap, but it improves the appearance of the floor without addressing flow, so lead times would change little. Decision We will phase in lean manufacturing line by line, beginning with line 2, which has the most repeat work. We will map the value stream, set a lead-time target for the line, and give the operators a role in choosing the improvements. We will start the next line only after the pilot line has held its lead time for a full quarter. Consequences The Head of Operational Excellence will lead the line 2 pilot and publish the value stream map and the results. Operators on the pilot line will be trained and will have time each week to propose and test improvements; we will fund that time. We will measure lead time, work-in-progress, rework, and on-time delivery on each line. During the rollout, some lines will work in the old way, and planning will need to take account of the differences. The pilot line's target is a lead time of 20 days; if we do not reach it we will find out why before extending to the next line. Related See Phase in Six Sigma for a data-driven approach that can complement lean.

records.title: Reposition the brand around reliability
records.text: Reposition the brand around reliability Status: accepted Date: 2026-01-15 Decision-maker(s): CMO Owner: Head of Brand Summary: We will reposition our core brand message from "innovative" to "reliable," reflecting where customer research shows we actually win and lose deals, with a phased rollout starting with sales collateral and paid channels. Issue Win/loss interviews over the last two quarters consistently show customers choosing us over faster-moving competitors specifically because of our uptime track record and support responsiveness — not because they perceive us as more innovative, which is our current brand positioning. Our messaging is actively working against the reason customers say they buy from us. Assumptions The reliability advantage is durable, not a temporary artifact of a competitor's recent outage. Existing brand equity built around "innovative" over the last three years is not so entrenched that repositioning will confuse existing customers. Sales and Customer Success can articulate the new positioning consistently once trained. Constraints No budget for a full rebrand (new logo, visual identity); this is a messaging repositioning within the existing visual system. Must not contradict claims already made in signed enterprise contracts referencing current messaging. Legal requires any reliability claims (e.g., uptime statistics) to be independently verifiable before publication. Options considered Keep "innovative" positioning, invest in proof points to make it more credible. Avoids repositioning risk, but doesn't address that win/loss data shows this isn't why customers actually choose us — this option optimizes the wrong message. Reposition fully around "reliable," phased rollout over two quarters. Aligns messaging with actual purchase drivers; phased approach limits risk if the shift underperforms. Run both messages in parallel, segmented by channel. Avoids committing fully, but brand consistency research suggests mixed messaging measurably weakens recall; two prior internal experiments with segmented messaging underperformed a single consistent message. Argument Win/loss data is the strongest signal we have of what customers actually value, and it points clearly at reliability. A phased rollout (collateral and paid channels first, full brand refresh deferred) lets us validate the new message's performance before committing budget we don't currently have to a full visual rebrand. Decision We will reposition core brand messaging around reliability, rolling out first through sales collateral and paid channels, with a full brand-refresh decision deferred pending performance data. Implications Head of Brand will update sales collateral and paid channel creative within one quarter. Legal will validate all uptime and reliability claims before any new asset ships. Sales and Customer Success will receive updated talking points and messaging training. A follow-on decision record will assess full visual rebrand investment once phase-one performance data is available, expected in two quarters. Existing signed contracts referencing "innovative" positioning are unaffected; this is a forward-looking messaging change only. Related decisions None superseded; this is the first formal repositioning decision on record for this brand element. Related notes Sales raised a concern that "reliable" could read as "boring" against a specific competitor's marketing; Head of Brand will test creative variants that pair reliability with a secondary differentiator before final rollout.

records.title: Choose between a product business and a service business
headings: Choose between a product business and a service business
records.text: Choose between a product business and a service business Status: accepted Date: 2026-07-08 Decision-maker(s): CEO and board Owner: Chief Strategy Officer Context We make most of our revenue (68%) from custom implementation projects for mid-sized customers, built on a software platform we own. Projects are profitable but unpredictable, and every one needs senior engineers, so growth is limited by hiring. Our platform is increasingly used without our services by partners, and investors are asking whether we are a product company or a services company. The answer changes what we hire, how we price, how we measure success, and what we say to customers. Options considered Become a product business. Sell the platform as a subscription with standard onboarding, and refer custom work to partners. Offers recurring revenue and growth that does not depend on headcount, but revenue would fall for roughly two years while we shift, and our best customers value the custom work. Stay a service business. Keep selling implementation projects and treat the platform as a tool for delivering them. Keeps the revenue and customer relationships we have, but leaves us exposed to hiring limits and to partners who deliver projects on our platform for less. Run both, with separate economics. Keep services as a distinct line with its own targets while the product line has its own roadmap, pricing, and measures. Keeps today's revenue while building a product business, but splits attention and risks leaving both lines under-invested. Decision We will become a product business over three years. We will move to subscription pricing with standard onboarding, shift the customer-facing implementation work to a partner network in stages, and keep a small services team for strategic customers. We will review the plan annually against subscription revenue, gross margin, and customer retention. Consequences The Chief Strategy Officer will publish the three-year plan, including the order in which customer segments move to subscription pricing. We expect total revenue to dip in the first two years; the board has agreed to this and to the investment needed to cover it. Roles will change as implementation work moves to partners; a separate decision will record how we support the people affected. We will measure ourselves differently: annual recurring revenue, gross margin, and net revenue retention replace project utilization as the headline measures. We give up control over some customers' implementation experience, in exchange for recurring revenue and growth that does not depend on hiring. Related This decision is tied to the target operating model in Adopt a target operating model, which will need updating to match.

records.title: Move to usage-based pricing
records.text: Move to usage-based pricing Status: accepted Date: 2026-04-05 Decision-maker(s): VP Product, with CFO sign-off Owner: Head of Pricing & Packaging Context Our current flat per-seat pricing under-monetizes our highest-usage customers and over-charges our lightest users, who are churning at 2x the rate of high-usage accounts. Three of our top five competitors have shifted to usage-based or hybrid pricing in the last 18 months, and prospects increasingly ask why we haven't. Options considered Keep flat per-seat pricing. No migration risk or customer disruption, but doesn't address the churn pattern among light users or the under-monetization of heavy users; competitively, we're increasingly the outlier. Move fully to usage-based pricing. Best aligns price with value delivered, but finance modeling shows meaningful revenue volatility quarter to quarter, and it's the most disruptive change for existing customers to absorb at once. Move to a hybrid model: a lower seat-based base fee plus usage-based overage. Smooths revenue volatility relative to full usage-based pricing while still fixing the light-user overcharge and heavy-user under-monetization; existing customers can be migrated with a grandfathering period. Decision We will move to a hybrid pricing model — reduced base seat fee plus usage-based overage — with new customers on the new model immediately and existing customers grandfathered for two quarters before migration. Consequences Existing customers must be individually modeled to confirm no one faces a net price increase during the grandfathering period without advance notice. Sales compensation plans need to be updated to reflect the new pricing structure before the new model goes live for new deals. Finance will revise revenue forecasting models to account for usage-based volatility. Customer Success will proactively communicate the change to at-risk light-usage accounts, since the new model should reduce (not increase) their bill. We accept short-term forecasting complexity in exchange for better price-to-value alignment and a stronger competitive position. Related Follow-on decision needed on exact overage pricing tiers — tracked separately as a pending pricing decision, not resolved in this record.

records.title: Build vs. buy for a project
headings: Build vs. buy for a project
records.text: Build vs. buy for a project Status: accepted Date: 2026-06-01 Decision-maker(s): COO Owner: Director of Operations Context We need a customer-facing scheduling tool for our services business. Our current process is manual, spreadsheet-based, and has caused three double-bookings in the last month that damaged customer relationships. We need a fix within one quarter and must decide whether to build this internally or buy an existing solution. Options considered Build in-house. Gives us exact fit to our specific scheduling rules and full control over the roadmap, but our engineering team estimates 3–4 months of dedicated work, which exceeds our one-quarter timeline and would pull capacity from two committed product initiatives. Buy an off-the-shelf scheduling platform. Available for implementation within 3–4 weeks; doesn't perfectly match every scheduling edge case we have, but covers roughly 90% of our documented requirements, with workarounds identified for the remaining 10%. Buy a platform and commission custom integration work from the vendor. Closes the requirements gap from the pure buy option, but adds 6–8 weeks and additional cost; two reference customers reported the vendor's custom integration timelines slipped significantly. Decision We will buy the off-the-shelf scheduling platform and manage the remaining 10% of edge cases with documented manual workarounds, revisiting a custom integration only if those workarounds prove unworkable in practice. Consequences Director of Operations will lead implementation and staff training within the 3–4 week vendor timeline. The 10% of scheduling edge cases not natively supported will be handled by documented manual process, reviewed after one quarter of live usage. We give up the exact fit a custom build would provide, in exchange for solving the double-booking problem well within this quarter instead of next. No engineering capacity is pulled from the two committed product initiatives, since this is a buy rather than a build. If manual workarounds prove unworkable after one quarter, a follow-on decision will evaluate the custom-integration option. Related This decision does not affect the two committed product initiatives' timelines, which was an explicit constraint on the options considered.

records.title: Adopt project portfolio management
records.text: Adopt project portfolio management Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-05 Decision-maker(s): Executive team Owner: Head of the Project Management Office Context We run about 90 active projects across six departments, and each department approves, staffs, and reports on its own. Leaders cannot see the total demand on shared people, such as our 14 data engineers, who are named on projects whose combined requests add up to more than twice their capacity. Projects stall waiting for the same few people, and low-value projects survive because no one compares them with the alternatives. We need a way to decide which projects to start, continue, or stop, based on strategy and capacity across the whole organization. Options considered Keep departmental decisions. No new process and full local autonomy, but it leaves the capacity conflicts and the lack of comparison unresolved. Create a central project portfolio office that approves every project. One view and consistent criteria, but every project would wait on one team, which becomes a bottleneck, and departments would feel the loss of control. Adopt portfolio management with a light central process. One shared list of projects with common scoring criteria (strategic fit, value, cost, risk, and the capacity needed), a quarterly portfolio review by the executive team to start, continue, or stop projects, and a rule that only projects above a set size need review. Gives one view and trade-offs made deliberately, without routing small work through a central team, but it needs reliable data from every department and a decision-making meeting that actually decides. Decision We will adopt project portfolio management with a light central process: one shared list of all projects above a set size (more than 200 person-days or 100,000 in cost), common scoring criteria, and a quarterly executive portfolio review that decides which projects to start, continue, or stop. Smaller projects stay under departmental control. Consequences The Head of the Project Management Office will keep the portfolio list, publish the scoring criteria within six weeks, and prepare each quarterly review. Each department will register its projects and its capacity by role, so the review sees demand against capacity and not demand alone. The executive team commits to deciding at the review, including stopping projects; stopped projects will be recorded with the reason. Departments give up some independence over larger projects in exchange for shared capacity being used on the highest-value work. We will review the process after two cycles, and measure the share of projects delivered on time, the number stopped early, and the use of shared teams. Related See Adopt a target operating model for how the portfolio process fits with shared services and customer-aligned teams.

records.title: Weigh public value in a service redesign
headings: Weigh public value in a service redesign
records.text: Weigh public value in a service redesign Status: accepted Date: 2026-06-18 Decision-maker(s): Director General, with the departmental board Owner: Director of Service Design Context Our agency processes about 400,000 benefit claims a year. Claims take a median of 38 days, and a recent review found that the people who wait longest are those least able to complete the online form: older people, people with limited English, and people without reliable internet access. A proposal would move all claims to a digital-only service and close two of the four local offices, saving an estimated 14% of operating cost. Because this is a public service, a choice that is efficient is not enough: it also has to be legitimate, fair, and something we can sustain, which are the three parts of the public value strategic triangle (legitimacy and support, public value created, and operational capacity). Options considered Digital-only service, with two local offices closed. Delivers the largest saving and the fastest median processing time for those who use it, but it shifts the burden onto the people who can least bear it and is likely to meet strong opposition from local representatives, which weakens legitimacy and support. Digital-first service, with assisted routes kept. Digital is the default, but the four offices stay open as assisted-digital centers, and a telephone route stays available. Gives most of the processing benefit while protecting access, but the saving is much smaller, about 5%. Keep the current mix and improve it. Make only process improvements. Lowest risk and no access concerns, but it leaves the 38-day median largely unchanged and does not use the opportunity digital tools offer. Decision We will build a digital-first service and keep the four offices as assisted-digital centers with a telephone route. We will judge the redesign on public value, not saving alone: median processing time, the gap in processing time between the slowest-served and the fastest-served groups, the number of successful first-time claims, and the saving. Consequences The Director of Service Design will publish the measures and report them quarterly, including the gap between the groups of claimants, to the departmental board and to the public. We accept a smaller saving (about 5% instead of 14%) in exchange for fair access and for legitimacy with local representatives and claimants. We will co-design the assisted-digital service with claimants who currently wait longest, and publish what we learned. We will revisit the office network only after the first year of data on who uses which route, and any proposal to close an office will be a new decision. Operational capacity: the assisted routes need trained staff, so training is funded before launch and not as an afterthought. Related See the Public Value Guide for the strategic triangle, social cost-benefit analysis, and equity considerations behind these measures.

records.title: Reduce single-vendor concentration risk
records.text: Reduce single-vendor concentration risk Status: accepted Date: 2026-05-20 Decision-maker(s): COO Owner: Head of Procurement Context An internal risk review found that 70% of our critical infrastructure spend runs through a single vendor. That vendor had an unplanned multi-hour outage last quarter that disrupted our customer-facing service, and their pricing has increased 18% year over year with no contractual cap. Continuing as-is leaves us exposed to both availability risk and unchecked cost growth. Options considered Accept the risk, do nothing differently. No near-term cost or effort, but leaves both the outage exposure and uncapped pricing risk fully in place; the risk review explicitly flagged this as unacceptable at current concentration levels. Renegotiate the existing contract for better SLAs and a pricing cap, stay single-vendor. Addresses pricing risk and improves accountability, but does not reduce single-point-of-failure exposure to another outage. Diversify: move 25% of critical workload to a second vendor over two quarters, renegotiate the primary contract for the remaining 75%. Reduces concentration risk meaningfully while avoiding the cost and disruption of a full migration; also strengthens our renegotiating position with the primary vendor. Decision We will diversify by migrating 25% of critical workload to a second vendor over the next two quarters, and renegotiate the primary vendor's contract for SLA commitments and a pricing cap on the remaining workload. Consequences Procurement will run a vendor selection process for the second vendor, using the same evaluation criteria as the original vendor selection. Engineering/Operations will need to plan a phased migration that avoids service disruption during the transition. The primary vendor's contract will be renegotiated in parallel; leverage from the diversification effort should improve renegotiation terms. We accept added operational complexity of managing two vendors in exchange for materially reduced outage and pricing risk. Head of Procurement will report concentration percentage and renegotiated SLA terms to the COO at the end of each quarter until the 25% migration is complete. Related This decision responds directly to the Q1 risk review findings; no prior decision record exists on vendor concentration to supersede.

records.title: Select a CRM platform
records.text: Select a CRM platform Status: accepted Date: 2026-02-02 Decision-maker(s): VP Sales Owner: Sales Operations Manager Context Our current CRM was implemented seven years ago and no longer supports the automation our sales process needs — reps spend an estimated 5 hours per week on manual data entry that competing tools automate. The contract renews in 90 days, giving us a natural switch point. Sales Operations, Marketing, and Finance all depend on this system and need to agree on the replacement. Options considered Renew current CRM, invest in custom automation add-ons. Avoids migration risk and retraining, but the vendor has confirmed no roadmap improvements to the underlying data model our automation gaps stem from — this treats the symptom, not the cause. Switch to Platform A. Strong marketing-automation integration (a current gap) and the best reference-call feedback on data migration support; standard implementation timeline is 8–10 weeks. Switch to Platform B. Lowest sticker price, but two reference calls independently raised concerns about support responsiveness during migration, and it lacks native integration with our finance system, which would require a custom connector. Decision We will switch to Platform A, with migration beginning immediately after contract termination notice is filed with the current vendor. Consequences Sales Operations will lead an 8–10 week migration, with a parallel-run period before full cutover. All reps require training before cutover; Sales Operations will schedule this in the two weeks prior. Current CRM contract must be terminated with required notice before the new term would otherwise auto-renew. We accept short-term productivity dip during migration and training in exchange for the automation gains projected to save each rep roughly 5 hours per week starting the following quarter. Marketing and Finance integrations will be validated in a staging environment before cutover, given Platform A's stronger reference feedback on migration support. Related Sales Operations will document the final migration runbook as a follow-on artifact once complete.

records.title: Phase in Six Sigma
records.text: Phase in Six Sigma Status: accepted Date: 2026-01-19 Decision-maker(s): Chief Operating Officer Owner: Head of Quality Context Our claims-processing operation handles 1.2 million cases a year, and about 7% of them need rework because of errors in data entry and routing. Rework costs an estimated 3.1 million a year and is a leading cause of customer complaints. Leaders want to use Six Sigma, the data-driven method for reducing variation and defects, to bring the rework rate down. Training everyone at once would take staff off the line, and our data is not yet good enough to measure defects consistently in every process. Options considered Company-wide rollout with belt training for all managers. Builds a shared method quickly, but removes many managers from operations for weeks and starts projects before we can measure them. Phase in with a small group of trained practitioners and one process first. Train a small group of Black Belts and Green Belts, choose one high-volume process (data entry), measure the defect rate, run a project, and use the result to choose the next. Slower, but it proves value with data and builds capability where it is needed. Use outside consultants to run projects. Fast, and experienced, but expensive and unlikely to leave internal capability behind. Decision We will phase in Six Sigma starting with one process: data entry for new claims. A small group of internal staff will be trained as Green Belts and Black Belts and will run a DMAIC (define, measure, analyze, improve, control) project on that process. We will extend to routing and then to other processes only after the data entry project has met its target for three consecutive months. Consequences The Head of Quality will sponsor the training, select the belts, and report results to the COO. The first project's target is to cut data-entry rework from 7% to below 3.5%, measured in the same way before and after. We will first invest in consistent measurement, because without reliable defect data the method cannot work. Managers outside the pilot will not be asked to run projects until their process is selected; this limits the disruption to operations. We accept a slower start than a company-wide rollout, in exchange for evidence and capability that stay in the company. Related See Phase in lean manufacturing for a related decision about reducing waste in a production setting.

records.title: Choose the primary database
records.text: Choose the primary database Status: accepted Date: 2026-03-22 Decision-maker(s): CTO Owner: Head of Platform Engineering Context Our current database is approaching scaling limits under projected 12-month growth, and the engineering team needs to choose its replacement before the next major product launch. This is included here as the one technology example in this set, to show that architecture decisions follow the exact same pattern as the business examples elsewhere in this collection — the discipline is general, not domain-specific. Options considered Vertically scale the current database. Lowest migration risk and no application changes required, but engineering estimates this buys only 6–9 months before hitting the same limits again, given projected growth. Migrate to Database A (managed, horizontally scalable). Addresses the scaling ceiling with strong vendor support and a well-documented migration path; adds recurring managed-service cost. Migrate to Database B (self-hosted, horizontally scalable). Lower recurring cost than the managed option, but requires building in-house operational expertise the team does not currently have, and reference checks with peer companies flagged higher operational overhead than expected. Decision We will migrate to Database A, the managed horizontally scalable option, prioritizing migration risk reduction and vendor support over the lower recurring cost of self-hosting. Consequences Platform Engineering will plan a phased migration with a parallel-run period before full cutover, to avoid disrupting the upcoming product launch. Recurring infrastructure cost increases; Finance has approved this as part of the growth investment budget. We give up the lower cost of the self-hosted option in exchange for avoiding the operational risk of building in-house expertise we don't currently have. A follow-on architecture decision will be needed on the connection-pooling and read-replica strategy once initial migration is complete. Related This decision responds to the same 12-month growth projection referenced in the current fiscal year's capacity planning; no prior database decision record exists to supersede.

records.title: Enter the mid-market segment
records.text: Enter the mid-market segment Status: accepted Date: 2026-03-10 Decision-maker(s): CEO, with Board approval Owner: VP Strategy Summary: We will extend our enterprise-only go-to-market to include the mid-market segment (100–1,000 employees), starting Q3, funded by reallocating 15% of the enterprise sales team's capacity. Issue Our enterprise pipeline has plateaued at roughly 40 qualified accounts per quarter in our addressable territories, while win rate has stayed flat for two years. Meanwhile, inbound interest from smaller companies (100–1,000 employees) has grown 3x year over year, and we currently turn this demand away or serve it poorly with an enterprise-configured sales motion. The board has asked for a credible growth path beyond enterprise account saturation. Assumptions Mid-market buyers convert faster (assumed 45-day average cycle vs. 120 days enterprise) but at roughly one-third the average contract value. Our product requires moderate simplification (fewer configuration steps) to be viable for mid-market self-serve onboarding. Existing enterprise sales talent is not optimized for a higher-velocity, lower-touch motion and would need retraining or augmentation. Constraints No net-new headcount approved for FY26; any mid-market motion must be funded from existing budget. Enterprise revenue targets for the current fiscal year are not to be put at risk. Legal has flagged that our current MSA terms assume enterprise-scale procurement cycles and will need a simplified version for faster-closing deals. Options considered Stay enterprise-only, invest further in enterprise expansion. Lowest execution risk, but doesn't address the plateau; several board members are skeptical this alone reaches next year's growth target. Enter mid-market via a dedicated new team, funded by new headcount. Cleanest execution, but blocked by the current-year hiring freeze. Enter mid-market by reallocating 15% of existing enterprise sales capacity, with a simplified onboarding motion. Slower ramp than a dedicated team, but fundable within current headcount and reversible within two quarters if it underperforms. Enter mid-market via a channel/reseller partnership instead of direct sales. Lowest internal cost, but reference calls with two peer companies indicated partner-led motions underperform direct sales by roughly 2x in the first year, and we'd cede the customer relationship. Argument The reallocation option is the only one that is both fundable under this year's constraints and reversible if the underlying assumption about mid-market conversion speed proves wrong. It also gives us real data on mid-market economics before committing to a dedicated team investment in FY27 budget planning, rather than committing headcount to an unproven motion. Decision We will enter the mid-market segment starting Q3, staffed by reallocating 15% of enterprise sales capacity into a mid-market pod, with a simplified onboarding flow and adjusted MSA terms for the segment. Implications VP Sales will identify which 15% of enterprise capacity moves, by end of Q2. Product will scope the onboarding simplification for a Q3 release. Legal will draft a simplified MSA variant for mid-market accounts. VP Strategy will report mid-market conversion and CAC data to the board at the end of Q3 and Q4, as the basis for a FY27 dedicated-team investment decision. Enterprise revenue targets remain unchanged; if the reallocation measurably harms enterprise pipeline, this decision will be revisited before FY27 planning. Related decisions Supersedes no prior decision; establishes a new segment strategy that FY27 headcount planning will build on. Related notes Two board members asked for a hard checkpoint at the end of Q4 rather than an open-ended pilot — captured above as the FY27 planning trigger.

records.title: Adopt a target operating model
records.text: Adopt a target operating model Status: accepted Date: 2026-09-15 Decision-maker(s): CEO and executive team Owner: Chief Operating Officer Context Over six years we grew from 60 to 450 people by acquisition and by hiring, and our organization now reflects that history rather than a plan: three business units run their own finance, support, and procurement processes, and customers meet different teams, systems, and prices depending on which unit they first contacted. Leaders cannot say who is accountable for end-to-end outcomes such as onboarding a customer. We need a target operating model (TOM) that describes how the organization will deliver its strategy: its processes, people, technology, locations, and governance. Options considered Keep the business-unit model and harmonize at the edges. Lowest disruption and keeps local autonomy, but it leaves duplicated functions in place (about 40 roles overlap) and does not give customers a single experience. Move to a functional model. Sales, delivery, finance, and support each become one company-wide function. Removes duplication and gives clear functional standards, but it separates teams from the customers and products they serve, and our two largest units told us delivery speed would suffer. Move to a hybrid model: shared services plus customer-aligned teams. Finance, people, procurement, and support become shared services; sales and delivery stay aligned to customer segments. Captures most of the efficiency of the functional model while keeping delivery close to customers, but it needs clear service levels between the shared services and the teams that depend on them, and it is the most complex to design. Decision We will adopt the hybrid model as our target operating model: shared services for finance, people, procurement, and support, and customer-aligned teams for sales and delivery. We will describe the target in one document covering processes, roles, technology, locations, and governance, and we will move toward it in stages, starting with the shared services that have the clearest duplication. Consequences The Chief Operating Officer owns the target operating model document and publishes the first version within eight weeks. Each shared service will publish service levels and a named owner before any team is moved to it, so the teams that depend on it know what to expect. Roles in the overlapping functions will change; a separate decision will record how we handle those changes, and no one will be told of an individual outcome before it is decided. Business-unit leaders give up some autonomy over support functions, in exchange for one customer experience and lower duplicated cost. We will review the model after four quarters against the measures set in the document: onboarding time, cost of shared services, and customer satisfaction by segment. Related The order and timing of the moves is a separate decision; see Phase in a business framework for how we approach staged change.

records.title: Adopt written ways of working
records.text: Adopt written ways of working Status: accepted Date: 2026-04-27 Decision-maker(s): Head of Engineering Owner: Engineering Manager Context Our product and engineering group has grown from 12 to 45 people in a year, and expectations that used to be understood are now different between teams: how quickly to answer a message, when a decision needs a meeting, how to disagree, and what counts as done. New joiners report that they learn these by making mistakes. We need ways of working that are explicit, understood, open to debate, and quick to flag when someone breaks them. Options considered Rely on culture and onboarding conversations. No effort, but it is the current approach, and it is already failing for people who join after the first cohort. Adopt one company-wide set of ways of working. One consistent set that everyone knows, but written by a few people and likely to feel imposed, and it would not suit the very different needs of design, engineering, and support. Write a short group-wide set and let each team add its own working agreement. A set of about ten shared principles and ground rules for the whole group, plus a team agreement that each team writes and reviews itself. Gives both consistency and ownership, but it takes team time and needs a place where agreements are kept and found. Decision We will write a short set of group-wide ways of working (about ten principles and ground rules) and require each team to keep its own written working agreement alongside them. All of them will be kept in the team documentation, reviewed every quarter, and open to change by anyone through a proposal that the team discusses. Consequences The Engineering Manager will draft the group-wide set within a month, circulate it for comment, and then publish it. Each team will write its agreement in its first two team meetings after publication and keep it where new joiners will find it on their first day. Every agreement names who handles a breakage, so people know what to do when a rule is not followed. We will check twice a year that people know the agreements and can say how to change them. Teams spend some time writing and reviewing agreements, which we accept in exchange for fewer misunderstandings. Related See Ways Of Working for examples of principles, ground rules, and team agreements.

records.title: Adopt workplace planning and management
records.text: Adopt workplace planning and management Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-08 Decision-maker(s): Chief Operating Officer Owner: Head of Workplace Context After we chose team-set anchor days for hybrid working, office use became much harder to predict: badge data shows 31% average use on a Monday and 74% on a Wednesday, and teams that share a floor have found no room to meet on the same day. Space, desks, meeting rooms, cleaning, and security are managed by three separate groups with separate data. We need a way to plan and manage the workplace as one system, using evidence of how it is used, so that the space fits the work and we spend our property budget well. Options considered Keep managing space by group. No change in effort, but decisions about space, bookings, and services continue to disagree with one another, and we cannot see the whole picture. Buy an integrated workplace management platform and let it assign desks. Complete data and automation, but it is costly, and automatic assignment ignores what teams need to be together. Plan the workplace from usage data, with team bookings. One owner for space, bookings, and services; badge, booking, and sensor-free data (no tracking of individuals); a quarterly plan of space by day; and bookable team zones. Matches space to demand and keeps teams together, but it needs one owner, a decision on what data to collect, and support from the teams. Decision We will plan and manage the workplace as one system under a Head of Workplace, using aggregated usage data from badge and booking systems (never individual tracking), a quarterly plan of space by day, and bookable team zones so that teams meet on the same days. We will review the amount of space we lease at the next break point using the first year of data. Consequences The Head of Workplace will own space, bookings, cleaning, and security services, and will publish the quarterly plan. We will report use only in aggregate, by floor and by day, and will not report on individuals; we will explain this to staff before collecting the data. Teams will book their zones for the days of their written agreements, so that anchor days actually bring people together. Desks and rooms will be fitted to the demand we measure, which may mean fewer fixed desks and more meeting and collaboration space. Adjustments for individuals follow Set a process for workplace reasonable adjustments and are not affected by desk booking rules. Related See Choose a hybrid working model for the policy this decision supports.

records.title: Set a process for workplace reasonable adjustments
headings: Set a process for workplace reasonable adjustments
records.text: Set a process for workplace reasonable adjustments Status: accepted Date: 2026-03-30 Decision-maker(s): Chief People Officer Owner: Head of Employee Experience Context In many places the law requires an employer to make reasonable adjustments so that a disabled employee or candidate is not at a disadvantage, and it is also simply the right way to treat people. Our requests are currently handled differently by each manager: some people wait weeks, some are asked to explain their condition repeatedly, and some are refused with no reason given. Managers also tell us they do not know what is reasonable or who pays. We need a clear process that is fast, private, and fair. Options considered Leave it to line managers. Keeps decisions close to the person and the job, but it produces inconsistent results, asks managers to make decisions they are not trained for, and exposes medical details to more people than needed. Send every request to a central team. Consistent and private, but it can be slow for simple requests such as a different chair or software, and the central team may not understand the role. A central team sets the process and pays, and managers make the decision on advice. The person describes what they need, not their diagnosis; the manager and the person agree an adjustment, using advice from a trained adviser where needed, with a central budget so cost does not decide the outcome. Fast for simple requests and consistent, but it needs training, an adviser, and a central budget. Decision We will adopt the third option: a central budget, a trained adviser, and decisions made between the person and their manager on the basis of what the person needs and not their diagnosis. Simple requests will be agreed within five working days, and any refusal must be given in writing with the reason and a route to appeal. Consequences The Head of Employee Experience will publish the process, the form, the expected timelines, and a guide for managers. Managers will be trained before they handle requests, and will not be told a diagnosis unless the person chooses to share it. A central budget pays for adjustments, so that team budgets do not decide outcomes; we will report the number, timing, and cost of requests each year without identifying individuals. Adjustments will be reviewed when the person's role or health changes, and not only when a problem arises. We accept the cost of the budget, the adviser, and manager training, in exchange for fairness, speed, and lower legal risk. Related This decision applies to hybrid working arrangements too; see Choose a hybrid working model. It does not replace local legal advice: requirements differ by jurisdiction.

records.title: Guide: Decision Records for Leaders
headings: Why leaders — not just engineers — should use decision records
Decision records apply to every part of the business
The anatomy of a decision record
records.text: Guide: Decision Records for Leaders This guide explains what a decision record is, why it matters to leaders across every function of a business, how to structure one, and how to run the practice well. Contents: What is a decision record? Why leaders — not just engineers — should use decision records Decision records apply to every part of the business The anatomy of a decision record The decision record lifecycle Roles and governance Best practices Common pitfalls Getting started in your organization Further reading What is a decision record? A decision record (DR) captures one significant choice: the situation that prompted it, the options weighed, the choice made, and the consequences expected. A decision log (DL) is the running collection of every decision record for a team, function, or organization — effectively an institutional memory of "why we do things this way." A decision record is not: A meeting minute (a record of what was discussed , not what was decided and why ). A project plan (a record of what happens next , not why this path was chosen over others ). A policy document (a record of a standing rule , though a decision record often produces one). It sits between these: a short, durable artifact that exists specifically so the reasoning behind a choice outlives the meeting where it happened. Why leaders — not just engineers — should use decision records Software teams adopted this practice first because code is expensive to unwind and new engineers constantly ask "why is it built this way?" Every leader faces the exact same dynamics: Institutional memory walks out the door. When a VP of Sales who chose the current territory model leaves, the reasoning leaves with them unless it was written down. Reorgs and leadership changes trigger re-litigation. Without a record, a new leader burns weeks re-debating a decision that was already carefully made — or worse, reverses it without realizing why it existed. Onboarding is faster with a "why," not just a "what." A new hire who can read the last dozen decisions in their function understands the organization's judgment, not just its current state. Writing it down improves the decision itself. Committing context, options, and trade-offs to a page — before deciding — surfaces gaps and unstated assumptions that a verbal discussion glosses over. It creates accountability without bureaucracy. A decision record names who decided, when, and why, which protects both the decision-maker (a documented, reasoned choice) and the organization (a clear owner to revisit if circumstances change). It scales communication across distance and time. For remote and asynchronous teams, and for stakeholders who weren't in the room, a well-written decision record does the work a live meeting would otherwise have to repeat. None of this is specific to software. It's specific to any decision that's costly to reverse, affects people beyond the decision-maker, or will plausibly be questioned later. Decision records apply to every part of the business Treat "decision record" as a genre, not a department's tool. The same six-part structure works whether the decision is architectural or commercial: Strategy Decision Record — market entry/exit, competitive posture, multi-year bets. Sales Decision Record — territory design, compensation plans, CRM/tooling choices, channel strategy. Marketing Decision Record — brand positioning, channel mix, agency vs. in-house, pricing communication. Product Decision Record — pricing model, roadmap trade-offs, build-vs-buy, sunset decisions. Project Decision Record — delivery methodology, vendor selection, scope trade-offs. Risk Decision Record — risk acceptance, mitigation, transfer, or avoidance, and the rationale. Human Resources Decision Record — policy changes (remote work, leveling, compensation bands), org design.
